newsitem.title: SPAIN: Countries meeting EMU criteria must join it -Spain.
newsitem.headline: Countries meeting EMU criteria must join it -Spain.

text.p: Spain will very likely meet the economic requirements for Europe's single currency and therefore cannot be excluded from the project's launch, Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo said on Thursday.

In one of the central bank governor's most-strongly worded statements yet, Rojo said failure to admit those nations that fulfil the criteria to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) could result in irreparable damage.
"A country that fulfils the criteria adequately cannot be excluded...the opposite would cause irreparable political damage," Rojo said at a seminar on the common currency.
He rated Spain's chances of meeting the criteria on deficit, debt, long-term debt and inflation levels, as well as currency stability, as "very high."
In the past year, Spain has gone from fulfilling none of the five criteria to meeting three, with the outlook positive for the other two, analysts said.
But some northern neighbours, particularly in Germany, have voiced concern that the improvement will prove fleeting.

Early this year, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the track record to join the euro's launch. Although he named no names, market participants believed he was targeting Italy, Spain and Portugal.

On Wednesday, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said that the sustainability of the criteria might lead to differentiation among the chances of Italy, Spain and Portugal to join the founding group of euro members.

In apparent response, Rojo said the reduction in Spain's public sector deficit, which is set to narrow to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year from 4.4 percent last year, in line with EMU requirements, was sustainable.

"The markets see it that way. The latest reports from Brussels, from the International Monetary Fund and from the Organisation of Economic and Cooperation and Development confirm the data, although this should not make us euphoric," Rojo said.
Spain has received high marks, particularly from the European Union, for its three-year economic stability plan through 2000.
